land.text: Goryeo, whose throne Yi Seong-gye took in 1392 ('Preceded by: Goryeo; Tamna' in the infobox), without Jeju

predecessors.note: Cliopatria ends Goryeo in 1394 and starts Joseon in 1395; the Goryeo dossier ends Goryeo in July 1392.

land.text: Jeju Island, put under firm central control by Taejong in 1404

predecessors.note: Joins in 1404, not at the founding; the infobox lists Tamna as a predecessor.

land.text: all of Joseon: 'replaced by the Korean Empire in 1897'; infobox 'Proclamation of the Korean Empire: October 13, 1897'

successors.note: Cliopatria starts the Korean Empire row in 1898.

capitals.name: Hanseong (Seoul)
capitals.note: Infobox: main capital Hanseong 1394-1399 and 1405-1897; Taejo moved the capital from Kaegyŏng.

capitals.name: Kaegyeong (Kaesong)
capitals.note: Jeongjong's 'first acts as monarch was to revert the capital to Kaegyŏng'; back to Hanseong in 1405 (infobox).

capitals.name: Hanseong (Seoul)
capitals.note: Seoul, from 1405 to the end of the kingdom; the court left for Ganghwa Island in 1627 and for Namhansanseong in 1636 only for the wars.

rulers.name: Gojong (Yi Jae-hwang / Yi Hui)
rulers.note: List of monarchs of Korea prints 1864-1897 for the Joseon row, then 1897-1907 as emperor of the Korean Empire; the Joseon page's text says he took the throne in 1863, its infobox says 1864.

correction.text: Goryeo's land as it stood when Yi Seong-gye took the throne in 1392 ('Preceded by: Goryeo; Tamna'), the Goryeo dossier's 1385 shape without Jeju

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's first Joseon shape begins in 1395 but the infobox dates Taejo's enthronement to 5 August 1392 and the renaming from Goryeo to 28 March 1393. For 1392-1394 the kingdom holds Goryeo's land; Jeju stays outside (see joseon_1395).

correction.text: the Cliopatria 1395 shape without Jeju, valid 1395-1403 only (Tamna autonomous until 1404)

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria's 1395 shape (208,185 km2) contains Jeju (10 cells). The Tamna page says 'the kingdom maintained local autonomy until 1404, when Taejong of Joseon placed it under firm central control', so Jeju is outside Joseon for 1395-1403 and the shape is right from 1404 (new keyframe joseon_1404). The Joseon page gives no area to compare. [orchestrator 2 Nov 2026: from/to set to 1395..1403 from this entry's own 'valid 1395-1403 only'; without them the compiler drew the shape for all its Cliopatria years, overlapping the next keyframe (window p1100-p1199 report)]

correction.text: the Cliopatria 1395 shape, with Jeju, for 1404-1414 (years only)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: from 1404 Jeju is Joseon's ('Taejong of Joseon placed it under firm central control and brought the Tamna kingdom to an end'; infobox 'Fall: 1404'), so the Cliopatria 1395 shape stands unchanged to 1414.

correction.text: the Cliopatria 1415 shape, unchanged, for 1415-1432 (years only)

keyframe_review.note: Shape unchanged (207,100 km2, 0.5% less than 1395 along the north-east edge; no page dates a border move in 1415) but only valid to 1432: the Joseon page dates the northern expansion to 1433 ('In 1433, Kim Chongsŏ's campaign expanded Korean territory, roughly the current border between North Korea and China'), whereas Cliopatria starts the larger shape in 1440. Joseon shapes carry the Jeju island from 1404.

correction.text: the Cliopatria 1440 shape, from 1433 (years only): 'roughly the current border between North Korea and China'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: the 1440 outline, 232,368 km2 against 207,100 km2 before, from 1433. The 142 extra cells are Chagang, Ryanggang, North Hamgyong and Rason, the Yalu and Tumen frontier ('the northernmost borders were expanded to the natural boundaries at the rivers of Amnok and Tuman'); 7 cells lie a river-cell across in Jilin and Liaoning, within the grid's precision. The page gives no area.
The Yalu-Tumen frontier shape (232,368 km2); valid from 1433 (see joseon_1433). The page gives no area figure for comparison.

235,001 km2: 11 more cells than 1440 (2 in Ryanggang and Chagang, 8 in Jilin across the Tumen and Yalu). The page puts the border on the two rivers ('Amnok and Tuman'); the Jilin cells are a river-cell wide and stay within the grid's precision. No page dates a change in 1516.
Same outline as 1516. Unchanged through the Imjin War's first year (1592); the ledger carries the Japanese occupation.

correction.text: the full 1600 outline for 1595-1599; the Japanese-held southeast coast is carried as occupation events, not by cutting the shape

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria cuts 170 cells (about 31,000 km2: Seoul, Gyeonggi, North Chungcheong, North Gyeongsang, Daegu, Busan, Ulsan) out of Joseon for 1595-1599. Pages say otherwise: the Japanese 'had been driven back to their network of fortresses, or wajo, on the southeastern Korean coast' (Sunch'on the westernmost), and the Joseon page records that Hanseong and Pyongyang were taken in 1592 and that the Japanese 'left most of the southern part of the Korean Peninsula occupied within months'. The kingdom's land is whole; the occupied coast is hatched through the ledger's occupation events (the warring-states-japan dossier has the matching events). The Japanese left on 16 December 1598 (Imjin War infobox), so the 1600 shape also holds for 1599.
235,001 km2, the same outline as 1516: the kingdom after the war (infobox of the Imjin War: 'Status quo ante bellum').

232,438 km2, 2,560 km2 less than 1600 (8 Jilin cells and a few edge cells). The Later Jin invasion page records no cession or occupation of land after the 1627 treaty, so the difference is edge noise at the Yalu.
231,872 km2: the same outline within two cells. No page dates a border change in 1632.

correction.text: the full 1640 outline for 1636-1639; the Qing occupation of December 1636 to January 1637 is carried as contest events

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria removes 164 cells (about 30,000 km2: most of North Pyongan, South Hwanghae, South Pyongan, Pyongyang, half of Gyeonggi and Seoul) for 1636-1639, as if the Qing kept the invasion route. The Qing invasion page records a Qing victory in which 'Joseon switches tributary allegiance from the Ming to the Qing', gives no territorial changes and no Qing garrisons, and says only that Qing forces occupied Hanseong (14 December 1636) and Ganghwa Island (27 January 1637) during the war, which ended on 30 January 1637. The land is whole; the occupation is a ledger event.

231,658 km2 for 1640-1859: the Yalu-Tumen border that the Qing and Joseon delegations settled in 1712 ('set the boundary at the Yalu and Tumen rivers'). The Jiandao shoal north of the Tumen was disputed and is outside the shape.

231,753 km2; the same outline as 1640 within one cell. The Russian frontier on the Tumen mouth (Cliopatria neighbour Russian Empire from 1860) is not described on the pages opened. The page gives no area.

Same outline as 1860. The Treaty of Shimonoseki (17 April 1895) 'officially guaranteed Korea's independence from China'; the kingdom was replaced by the Korean Empire on 13 October 1897, the date that the Joseon dossier ends.

region.text: the kingdom of Goryeo, which Taejo took over (infobox 'Preceded by: Goryeo; Tamna')

ledger.note: 1392: Yi Seong-gye is enthroned as King Taejo, founding the Joseon dynasty on Goryeo's land. Infobox 'Enthronement of Taejo: August 5, 1392'; 'was founded by Taejo of Joseon in 1392'. The page gives no boundary; the region is Goryeo's last shape.
1393: the kingdom is renamed Joseon. Infobox 'Country renamed from Goryeo to Joseon: March 28, 1393'; the lead says 'Korea was retitled and the capital was moved to modern-day Seoul'.
1394: the capital moves from Kaegyeong to Hanseong (Seoul). Infobox 'Main: Hanseong (now Seoul) (1394-1399/1405-1897)'; 'Temporary: Kaegyŏng (1392-1394/1399-1405)'.
1399: Jeongjong returns the court to Kaegyeong. 'First acts as monarch was to revert the capital to Kaegyŏng' (Joseon page); Hanseong is again the capital from 1405 (infobox).

region.text: the island of Jeju, the Tamna kingdom

ledger.note: 1404: Taejong of Joseon ends the autonomy of Tamna (Jeju). 'the kingdom maintained local autonomy until 1404, when Taejong of Joseon placed it under firm central control and brought the Tamna kingdom to an end'; infobox 'Fall: 1404'; in 1402 the last lord Go Bong-rye 'voluntarily relinquished his title of seongju to the king'.
1405: the court returns to Hanseong for good. Infobox 'Main: Hanseong (1394-1399/1405-1897)'.

region.text: the north-east and north up to the Amnok (Yalu) and Tuman (Tumen) rivers, taken from the Jurchens

ledger.note: 1433: Kim Chongsŏ's campaign pushes the frontier to the Yalu and Tumen. 'In 1433, Kim Chongsŏ's campaign expanded Korean territory, roughly the current border between North Korea and China'; the lead says the northernmost borders reached 'the natural boundaries at the rivers of Amnok and Tuman'. Sejong's 'four forts and six posts' against the Jurchens have no year on the page. Cliopatria starts the larger shape in 1440. The region is the difference between Cliopatria's 1440 and 1415 shapes (Chagang, Ryanggang, North Hamgyong, Rason).

region.text: Busan and the Gyeongsang coast, where the First Division landed on 23 May 1592

ledger.note: 1592: Hideyoshi's army lands on the south-east coast of Korea. 'On 23 May 1592, 7,000 Japanese soldiers of the First Division, led by Konishi Yukinaga' (infobox 'Date: 23 May 1592 - 16 December 1598'); the page then follows the advance through the Gyeongsang towns. The Japanese side of this event is in warring-states-japan.
1592: the Japanese take Hanseong. 'Konishi arrived at Hanseong first, on 10 June'; 'The First Division found the castle undefended with its gates locked, as King Seonjo had fled the day before.'
1592: the Japanese take Pyongyang. 'On 20 July 1592, the First and Third Divisions entered the deserted city of Pyongyang.'

1593: the Japanese leave Hanseong. The Imjin War page is silent on the date (it gives Katō Kiyomasa's withdrawal from Hamgyong 'to Hanyang on 29 February' without a year, and dates no leaving of Hanseong); the Joseon page puts Ming China's intervention in 1593 and says the Japanese 'left most of the southern part of the Korean Peninsula occupied'. The warring-states-japan dossier (another batch) dates the retreat to January 1593 from the Azuchi-Momoyama page.

1593: the Japanese leave Pyongyang and the north. The Imjin War page gives no date for the retreat; the Joseon page dates the Ming intervention to 1593, and the Noryang page has the Japanese 'driven back to their network of fortresses, or wajo, on the southeastern Korean coast'.

region.text: the wajo on the south-east coast from Busan to Sunch'on

ledger.note: 1598: the Japanese leave Korea. 'On 18 September 1598, Hideyoshi unexpectedly died'; the forces 'were ordered to withdraw back to Japan'; Noryang on 16 December 1598 and 'The last ships sailed to Japan on 24 December'. The wajo held to the end ran from Busan to 'The Sunch'on wajo was the westernmost Japanese fortress'.

region.text: the north-west from Uiju to Pyongyang

ledger.note: 1627: the Later Jin invades from the north. 'On 14 January, the Jurchen army advanced into Uiju'; the fortress of Neunghan fell on 21 January and 'Pyongyang fell without a fight'; King Injo fled Hanseong for Ganghwa Island. The region is the invasion route, from the Yalu to Pyongyang, my reading of the page's towns.

region.text: the north-west from Uiju to Pyongyang

ledger.note: 1627: the Later Jin withdraws. Infobox 'January - 3 March 1627'; 'The Jin army then withdrew to Mukden, ending the three-month-long invasion'; the Ganghwa terms say 'The Later Jin and Joseon will not violate each other's territory'; no land was ceded.

region.text: Hanseong and Ganghwa Island, occupied by the Qing during the war

ledger.note: 1636: the Qing invade and take Hanseong. 'On 9 December 1636, Hong Taiji led Manchu, Mongol, and Han Chinese Banners in a three pronged attack on Joseon'; 'On 14 December, Hanseong's garrisons were defeated, and the city was taken.' The Qing proclaimed in 1636; Cliopatria's row for them is the Later Jin Dynasty to 1644. Cliopatria's shape for 1636-1639 cuts a corridor from the Yalu to Seoul that the page does not describe.

1637: Injo surrenders and Joseon becomes a Qing tributary. 'Dorgon occupied Ganghwa Island on 27 January... King Injo surrendered the day after' (infobox end 30 January 1637; result 'Joseon switches tributary allegiance from the Ming to the Qing'); no cession of land.

region.text: the whole of Joseon, passing to the Korean Empire

ledger.note: 1897: the Joseon court proclaims the Korean Empire and Gojong becomes emperor. Infobox 'Proclamation of the Korean Empire: October 13, 1897'; lead: 'replaced by the Korean Empire in 1897'.

wars.name: Ōei Invasion of Tsushima
wars.outcome: Sejong 'launched the punitive Ōei Invasion against Tsushima' in 1419 with 227 ships and some 17,000 soldiers; after 15 days of fighting the lord of Tsushima surrendered. The page records no change of territory.
wars.note: Listed so the reviewer can see it was considered; the page's Tsushima section is cut off mid-sentence and the 1443 treaty is not on it.

wars.name: Joseon campaigns against the Jurchens (Four Forts and Six Posts)

zones.text: the north and north-east up to the Amnok and Tuman rivers

wars.outcome: 'In 1433, Kim Chongsŏ's campaign expanded Korean territory, roughly the current border between North Korea and China'; Sejong 'established four forts and six posts' against the Jurchens (no year).
wars.note: Only 1433 is dated on the page; the forts and posts were built over several years and the Sejong and Kim Jongseo pages are silent on them. A gap-filler should open a page on the Four Forts and Six Garrisons (neither 'Four Forts and Six Posts' nor 'Four Forts and Six Garrisons' loads).

wars.name: Imjin War

zones.text: the capital and Pyongyang, held for months in 1592-1593

wars.outcome: Joseon and Ming victory; 'Status quo ante bellum'. The Japanese took Hanseong and Pyongyang in 1592, were driven back to the wajo on the south-east coast, and left in December 1598.
wars.note: The Imjin War page loads only to July 1592 (the text is cut at the naval fighting off Okpo); 1593-1598 rest on the Noryang page. The Japanese retreat from Hanseong is not dated on either.

wars.name: Later Jin invasion of Joseon
wars.outcome: Later Jin victory. Joseon abandoned the Ming era name Tianqi, sent Yi Gak as hostage, and opened border markets; the Jin withdrew to Mukden by 3 March 1627 and took no land.

wars.name: Qing invasion of Joseon
wars.outcome: Qing victory, 9 December 1636 to 30 January 1637; Joseon ended its use of the Ming-era name, sent two princes as hostages, accepted the Qing calendar and paid tribute every year; no land was ceded.
wars.note: The Qing took the imperial title in 1636; Cliopatria's row for the same state is Later Jin Dynasty (1619-1644), then Qing Dynasty from 1645.

wars.name: First Sino-Japanese War
wars.outcome: A war 'between Japan and the Qing Empire, fought largely in Korea'; the infobox dates the Japanese occupation to 23 July 1894 and the Treaty of Shimonoseki to 17 April 1895, which 'officially guaranteed Korea's independence from China'.
wars.note: Joseon was the battleground, not a belligerent; no land changed hands. The page does not name the places fought over.

certainty.note: The northern frontier against the Jurchens is approximate until the 1433 campaign; the south and the coasts are sea frontiers.
The Amnok and Tuman rivers are named as the border but not surveyed; the Jurchen and Ming side of the Changbai mountains was not delimited.

The 1712 Mount Paektu stele set the boundary at the Yalu and Tumen rivers; the Tumen source and the Jiandao shoal north of the river stayed disputed and are the exception (the 1885-1887 talks did not settle it).

notes: Wikidata: Cliopatria's Joseon row shares Q28405 with Gojoseon (Old Joseon, legendary 2333 BCE to 108 BCE); they are different states 1,500 years apart, so no merge; the shared id looks like a Wikidata mix-up (the Gojoseon dossier of the sibling batch says the same). Cliopatria rows: shapes 1595-1599 and 1636-1639 are wrong (see the keyframe notes): the first draws the Japanese path from Seoul to Busan as lost, the second the Qing invasion route, whereas the pages record occupation of the south-east coast (1592-1598) and of Hanseong and Ganghwa Island (1636-1637), not loss of territory. The shape 1415-1439 should stop in 1432 and the Yalu-Tumen shape start in 1433; Jeju is outside the 1395 shape until 1404. Cliopatria's relation 'Allegiance of Joseon to Ming Dynasty' (1395-1571) is not recorded here because the suzerain owns the vassal events (a vassal_start with counterpart joseon in the Ming and Qing dossiers). What the pages give: Joseon 'joined the Imperial Chinese tributary system in 1401' (Joseon page; infobox 'tributary relations with the Ming and Qing 1401-1895'); Injo 'was forced to end his relations with the Ming and recognize the Qing as suzerain' (Joseon page), result 'Joseon switches tributary allegiance from the Ming to the Qing' on 30 January 1637 (Qing invasion page); the Treaty of Shimonoseki, 17 April 1895, 'officially guaranteed Korea's independence from China' (Joseon page). Cliopatria ends the Ming allegiance in 1571, which no page supports. Suzerain slugs: ming-dynasty (ea-07), later-jin-dynasty/qing-dynasty (ea-08). Pages that did not load: Four_Forts_and_Six_Posts, Four_Forts_and_Six_Garrisons, Japanese_invasions_of_Korea_(1592-98) in two spellings. The Imjin_War page loads only up to July 1592 even with offsets, so 1593-1598 rest on Battle_of_Noryang; the date of the Japanese retreat from Seoul and Pyongyang is therefore confidence 1. The Sejong and Kim Jongseo pages are thin on the Four Forts and Six Posts: the 1433 date is the Joseon page's. Nothing dates the second invasion of 1597 (Jiksan) on the pages opened. Counterparts needing a dossier: jurchens (1433 gain; the Jurchen tribes beyond the Tumen, cited by the Goryeo dossier too), later-jin-dynasty is a Cliopatria row (ea-08). Gazetteer names used that the gazetteer lacks: place Suncheon (South Jeolla, 127.49 E, 34.95 N, the westernmost wajo). Page budget: nine pages for the Joseon article, wars and border; the Tamna page was a tenth, opened to settle the Jeju overlap with the Tamna dossier. Not covered: Joseon-Russia frontier at the Tumen mouth from 1860, the Treaty of Ganghwa (26 February 1876, three ports opened, no land), Ulleungdo and Dokdo, the Qing garrisoning of Jiandao, and the Gihae/Gyehae Tsushima settlements.
